claims.text: High-throughput computational screening integrated with tailored thermal treatments can achieve phase stability, microstructure refinement, and optimized mechanical properties in high-entropy alloys.
The integrated method works by promoting finely dispersed nanoscale precipitates.
The relevant material system includes arc-melted Al-Cr-Fe-Mn-Ti high-entropy alloys.
The initial alloy has a mixed BCC matrix with potential for L21 phase formation.
High-throughput screening can select compositions using criteria such as melting temperature above 1250 °C and targeted L21 phase fractions.
A suitable processing sequence includes arc melting, homogenization at about 1200 °C, and annealing at about 700 °C for 2 hours.
The specified homogenization and annealing sequence produces the desired nanoscale precipitate microstructure.
The method is applicable throughout a composition window with Al below 25 at.% and Mn above 15 at.%.
The resulting structure consists of nanoscale L21 precipitates or ordered antiphase domains embedded in a softer BCC matrix.
The L21 precipitates or ordered antiphase domains strengthen the alloy through ordering strengthening, dislocation impediment, and load transfer.
Controlled thermal treatments restrict excessive precipitate coarsening.
A refined precipitate microstructure boosts mechanical properties, particularly yield strength at elevated temperatures.
Screening-guided and thermally treated alloys will have finer and more uniformly distributed nanoscale precipitates than conventionally processed alloys.
The intervention will increase high-temperature yield strength by approximately 100 MPa or more under comparable test conditions.
Alloys produced without computational screening and controlled thermal treatments typically have less refined precipitate structures and lower high-temperature mechanical performance.
Benefits may not be realized outside the stated composition and processing regimes.
Yield-strength improvement and precipitate-size distributions are sensitive to minor variations in composition and processing.
Uncertainty in the thermodynamic database may alter the optimal processing window.
Elevated-temperature compression testing at approximately 600-700 °C is suitable for measuring the proposed strength outcome.
Failure to obtain statistically significant precipitate refinement and a corresponding strength improvement over the control would falsify the hypothesis.
